content: It is not feasible to provide comprehensive physical or psychosocial care for patients and their families in a hospital setting. However, when patients and healthcare staff are present in the same location, it facilitates training and education. Donors can directly observe the impact of their contributions, and volunteers can gather, fostering a sense of belonging. Highly skilled medical and nursing care, if offered, represents the most expensive form of palliative care, potentially costing as much or more than hospital care. Many patients prefer to receive care or pass away in their own homes rather than in a hospice. Practical challenges, such as distance, cost, or convenience, may limit the frequency of family visits. Additionally, if a hospice experiences a high number of deaths, it may unsettle patients and lead to the facility being labeled as a death house. Hospice day-care services allow patients to remain at home while receiving specialized care at a hospice during the day. This arrangement can provide custodial care for patients when family members are at work, enabling them to stay at home until they are no longer able to travel. Transportation, such as ambulances equipped with wheelchair facilities or stair crawlers, may be necessary unless the family can transport the patient. Travel time and distance can be limiting factors, and patients may feel exhausted upon reaching the day-care center. Group activities offered in such settings may not suit all patients. Education centers benefit from having patients concentrated in one location, providing ample clinical material for teaching. Proper facilities can accommodate groups of trainees, but patient and family privacy must be safeguarded. Clinical staff involved in teaching may need a reduced workload, and hiring trained teaching staff incurs additional costs. Research centers attract high-caliber staff due to their academic culture, but research requires significant time and financial investment. Most clinicians are not trained in research and require additional training. Dedicated time and staff are essential for conducting research. Palliative care centers or hospices must clearly define the types of patients they will accept, as this determines the care provided. For example, some centers may focus on cancer patients, others on HIV/AIDS, strokes, or dementia, while others accept patients with any chronic, life-limiting condition. Decisions must also be made regarding whether to accept children, adults, or both. The prognosis of patients may also guide the focus of care, whether it is based on survival and recovery or solely on the need for palliative care. Admission and discharge criteria are essential, and mechanisms should be in place for patients to return to the hospice program during crises. Geographical location is particularly important for home care, as staff travel time limits the catchment area. For inpatient hospice care, accessibility for visiting family members may also be a limitation. Technology, such as computers and mobile devices, can support patients in rural and remote areas. Socioeconomic conditions may also influence the focus of palliative care centers, with some serving the very poor or homeless. While universal coverage is the goal, limited resources may constrain care for all. Family involvement varies, with some centers allowing family members to stay with the patient, while others permit only visits. Decisions must also be made regarding the maximum number of guests allowed per patient. Before establishing a palliative care service, clarity is needed on the mix of paid staff and volunteers, as well as the required professional expertise. Needs vary depending on the type of service provided. For home care, a nurse often serves as the main care manager, coordinating additional resources as needed. In resource-rich settings, an interdisciplinary team with a coordinator is typically present. Special training in symptom assessment and case management is essential, in addition to nursing expertise. In inpatient services, nursing staff with varying levels of expertise are available 24/7, forming the largest group in the interdisciplinary team. Day-care services may be managed by an occupational therapist, physiotherapist, or nurse manager, with medical input depending on available resources. This input may come from a palliative care specialist or general physicians with some palliative care training. Centers of excellence and training require specialist palliative care physicians and nurses. If recruiting and retaining highly trained specialists is challenging, options such as joint appointments or service-level agreements with hospital palliative care services may be necessary. Medical social workers and counselors are core members of the hospice team, and junior staff may require mentoring from experienced workers. Allied health professionals, such as occupational, physiotherapy, and speech therapists, may be needed part-time or full-time and require training in managing patients with advanced disease. Volunteers play a vital role in hospice services, enriching care and sometimes forming the main workforce. However, training and coordination are necessary, and volunteers are not without cost. They can also assist with governance, fundraising, administration, and maintenance. The reliable availability of essential medications, particularly oral morphine, is crucial for pain and symptom management. In many countries where palliative care is underdeveloped, such medications are only available in hospitals, requiring collaboration with hospital staff to provide them for home or hospice patients. Funding for palliative care services may come from foundations, public donations, legacies, government subsidies, co-payments by end-users, or a combination of these sources. Many palliative care centers or hospices begin as community projects funded by charitable organizations. For sustainability, government funding should be sought to cover part or all of the services provided, as the goal is to integrate palliative care into the health system. Public fundraising is also beneficial, promoting community awareness and ownership. Examples from Kerala, India, and Costa Rica highlight the importance of diverse funding sources, including public funds, charitable contributions, and government support. External support plays a role in training, funding, and workforce development in lowand middle-income countries where palliative care services are not yet established. Initiatives such as training-of-trainers programs, overseas clinical fellowships, and embedding trained professionals in local units can help build capacity. However, sustainability from local resources must be addressed from the outset. Case studies from Romania, Kenya, and other countries demonstrate the importance of integrating palliative care into existing health systems. Successful integration requires leadership, stakeholder engagement, and innovative approaches to service delivery. For example, modular training programs, community sensitization, and partnerships with local businesses have been effective in expanding palliative care services. Integration also involves embedding palliative care within the healthcare continuum, making it an essential component of primary care rather than a separate specialty. In summary, a comprehensive approach to palliative care requires national policies, availability of essential medicines, and integration into the health system. Successful implementation depends on leadership, stakeholder engagement, and innovative service delivery models.
